title: Free Will and Grace
lead: Can fallen people choose to turn to God, or must God's grace act first? The Bible calls people to choose, and it also says God draws, hardens and opens hearts. The question has been debated from Augustine and Pelagius to Luther and Erasmus, Calvinists and Arminians, and it still divides the churches.

sections.b: Moses tells Israel, "Life and death are what I have put before you, blessing and curse. Choose life, then" (Deuteronomy 30:19). Joshua tells the tribes to "decide for yourselves today who it is you will serve" (Joshua 24:15). The prophets plead with Israel to turn and live (Ezekiel 18:31–32), and Jesus mourns over Jerusalem: he wanted to gather its people, but they were not willing (Matthew 23:37). Paul says God wants all people to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4). Such passages seem to assume that people can answer God's call.
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 30:19; Joshua 24:15; Ezekiel 18:31–32; Matthew 23:37; 1 Timothy 2:4; Isaiah 55:6–7

sections.b: Other passages stress human inability and God's prior work. Jeremiah asks whether a leopard can change its spots (Jeremiah 13:23). God hardens Pharaoh's heart (Exodus 9:12) and promises to give Israel a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26; Deuteronomy 30:6). Jesus says no one can come to him unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). Paul says people were dead in sin before God made them alive (Ephesians 2:1–5), that God has mercy on whom he wills (Romans 9:15–18), and that God works in believers both to will and to act (Philippians 2:12–13). Joseph's word to his brothers, "You planned evil against me, but God planned it for good" (Genesis 50:20), shows human choice and God's purpose in the same act.
sections.refs: Jeremiah 13:23; Exodus 9:12; Ezekiel 36:26; Deuteronomy 30:6; John 6:44; Ephesians 2:1–5; Romans 9:15–18; Philippians 2:12–13; Genesis 50:20

sections.b: Around AD 400 the British monk Pelagius taught that people can obey God by their own natural powers; Augustine answered that since Adam's fall the will is bound by sin and only grace can free it. Councils at Carthage (418) and Orange (529) sided with Augustine. In 1525 Luther wrote The Bondage of the Will against Erasmus, who defended a free choice that cooperates with grace. In the Netherlands, followers of Jacob Arminius taught that God's grace can be resisted, and the Synod of Dort (1619) rejected their view. John Wesley later taught "prevenient grace," a grace given to all that frees the will enough to accept or refuse salvation. Jewish tradition has long held both truths together, as in Rabbi Akiva's saying in Mishnah Avot that all is foreseen, yet freedom of choice is given.

Catholic teaching, set out at Trent, holds that the fall weakened free will but did not destroy it; grace comes first, and the will freely cooperates with it. Orthodox theology speaks of synergy, God and the person working together, and never accepted Augustine's full teaching on the bound will. Lutherans teach that before conversion the will cannot choose God, but they reject the idea that God chooses some for damnation. Reformed churches teach that fallen people cannot turn to God until he gives them new life, and that his saving call cannot finally be resisted. Methodists, Pentecostals and other Arminian churches hold that prevenient grace enables every person to respond. Baptists include both Calvinist and non-Calvinist traditions. See also Election and God's Hidden Care.

common: Christians agree that salvation begins with God's grace and that people are responsible for how they respond.
uncommon: Open theists hold that God has chosen not to know every future free choice in advance.
